intro: Every long story is heading somewhere. In this last unit you read the ancient texts about where the Bible's story ends. Psalm 82 puts the gods of the nations on trial. Daniel 7 gives a kingdom to the holy ones. Paul calls believers adopted children and heirs. Revelation ends with a battle, a bound dragon, and a garden city whose gates never shut.

You will read the documents first: the Hebrew Bible and the Septuagint, a Dead Sea Scroll, Jubilees and 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, the New Testament, and church fathers such as Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius and Augustine. Then you will meet the researchers who read them: Mullen and Smith on the divine council, Collins on Daniel, Clifford on the holy mountain, Beale and Bauckham on Revelation, and Michael Heiser on God's family and Har Magedon.

By the end you will be able to explain what these texts promise the people they call children of God, and why readers of every tradition say those people never become equal to God. You will be able to trace a word from Hebrew into Greek, compare a symbol with its older source, and describe a debate fairly without taking a side.
bigQuestion: What do the ancient texts say about the end of the story, from God's children raised to honor to the nations healed, and how do different readers understand them?

chapters.title: Believers as God's Family
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the ancient texts say the people called children of God will become, and how do readers keep that from meaning they become God?

story.title: Is It Not Written, Ye Are Gods?
story.kicker: A student reading John 10 for a class finds Jesus quoting a psalm that calls someone gods, and she has to find out why.
paragraphs: Rosa had a simple assignment for her senior seminar: read John chapter 10 and write one question about it. She expected the shepherd verses. She had heard those before. Then, near the end of the chapter, she stopped. In the King James Version, Jesus answers a crowd with a question of his own: 'Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?' She read it three times.

The footnote pointed her to Psalm 82:6. She opened the psalm. It was only eight verses long. God stands in a gathering and judges beings the psalm calls gods. Then comes the line Jesus quoted: 'I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.' The next verse says they will die like men. Rosa wrote in her margin: Who are these gods, and why would Jesus bring them up?

Her teacher, Mr. Okafor, did not give her one answer. He gave her three. Many older Christian commentators read the gods as human judges. Some rabbinic writings connect the verse with Israel receiving the Torah at Sinai. And many modern scholars, from E. Theodore Mullen in 1980 to Michael Heiser in 2015, read Psalm 82 as a scene in God's heavenly council, with heavenly beings on trial.

Then he handed her a small stack of photocopies. There was Daniel 7, where a kingdom is given to 'the saints of the most High.' There was a page of 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, promising the righteous a place with the hosts of heaven. There was a description of a Dead Sea Scroll that reads Psalm 82 about a heavenly figure named Melchizedek. 'Start with these,' he said. 'Then see what the scholars do with them.'

Rosa changed her question. It was no longer only about John 10. It was now: What do the old texts say believers will become, and how do different readers keep that from sounding like people turning into God? This chapter follows her question through the documents.
story.think: Why might a teacher hand a student the ancient texts before the scholars' books? What does a reader gain by meeting the documents first?

lessons.title: Two Families, One Household
lessons.mainIdea: Job 38:7 and Genesis 1:26–27 picture heavenly sons of God and humans made in God's image, and some scholars read them as two families meant to share one home.
reading: Job 38:7 describes the morning the earth was founded. The *sons of God* shouted for joy, the text says, while the morning stars sang together. The scene has an audience before any human appears. The Hebrew Bible pictures God already surrounded by heavenly beings when creation begins. Scholars call this gathering the *divine council*, the assembly of heavenly beings around God's throne, seen also in 1 Kings 22:19 and Psalm 82:1.

Genesis 1:26–27 then has God say, 'Let us make man in our image.' Readers have long asked who 'us' is. Early Christian writers often read it as the Trinity. The medieval Jewish commentator Rashi read it as God speaking with his heavenly court. Many Old Testament scholars today read the *image of God* as a royal role: humans are placed on earth to represent God, the way a king's statue stood for the king in his lands.

Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), joined these passages into one picture. He read God as having two families, one heavenly and one human, meant to meet in Eden. In his reading, both families had rebels, and the Bible's story aims to restore one household. Other scholars describe the Bible's big story with different themes, such as covenant, kingdom or salvation history. Many see these themes as overlapping rather than competing.

the scholarly term for the gathering of heavenly beings around God in texts like Psalm 82 and 1 Kings 22
the phrase in Genesis 1:26–27 for how humans are made; many scholars read it as a role of representing God on earth

lessons.title: The Nations Given Away
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:8 reads 'sons of Israel' in the Masoretic Text but 'sons of God' at Qumran and 'angels of God' in the Septuagint, and scholars read the older wording as nations placed under heavenly rulers.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 says that when the Most High divided the nations, he set their borders by a number. The copies disagree about the number. The *Masoretic Text*, the standard medieval Hebrew text, says 'the sons of Israel.' A Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4 reads 'the sons of God.' The *Septuagint*, the old Greek translation, reads 'the angels of God' in Brenton's English of 1844. Most text critics today think 'sons of God' is the older wording.

Other ancient Jewish writers knew this picture of nations under heavenly rulers. Daniel 10:13 and 10:20 speak of a 'prince of Persia' and a 'prince of Grecia' who oppose a heavenly messenger. The Book of *Jubilees*, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, says in chapter 15 that God placed spirits in authority over all the nations. Over Israel, it says, he set no angel or spirit, because he alone rules them.

Scholars read the older wording in more than one way. Mark S. Smith, in The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001), argued that Deuteronomy 32:8–9 keeps an old picture in which the Most High gives each divine son a nation and the LORD receives Israel. Other scholars read the Most High and the LORD as one God in these verses. Readers who follow the Masoretic reading usually see the verse as a statement about Israel's place among the peoples.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied and marked by scribes called Masoretes in the Middle Ages
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun in Egypt in the third century BCE
a Jewish retelling of Genesis and early Exodus from the second century BCE, translated into English by R. H. Charles (1917)

lessons.title: The Rebels Replaced
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 82 sentences the gods of the nations, and Daniel 7 gives the kingdom to the holy ones of the Most High; readers debate who those holy ones are.
reading: Psalm 82:7 ends the trial of the gods with a verdict: they will die like men and fall like one of the princes. They had judged unjustly and ignored the poor (Psalm 82:2–4). Psalm 82:8 then asks God himself to rise and judge the earth, 'for thou shalt inherit all nations' in the King James Version. The psalm moves from rulers who failed to God taking the nations back.

Daniel 7 carries the picture further. 'One like the Son of man' comes to the *Ancient of Days* and receives a kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Later in the chapter the kingdom is given to 'the saints of the most High' (Daniel 7:18, 27). A Dead Sea Scroll called the War Scroll hopes for something similar: the rule of the angel Michael among the heavenly beings, and the rule of Israel among all people.

Scholars debate who the *saints of the Most High* are. John J. Collins, in his commentary Daniel (1993), read the 'holy ones' as angels, with 'the people of the holy ones' as faithful Israel on earth. Other scholars read the saints as faithful Israel itself. Michael Heiser read these texts together as a *displacement*: faithful humans take the places of the fallen gods of the nations, raised to honor in God's council. Many readers describe the same passages as God's kingdom coming through Israel's Messiah.

words.d: Heiser's picture of faithful humans taking over the places of rule once held by rebellious heavenly beings
the title for God seated on the throne in the vision of Daniel 7
the holy ones who receive the kingdom in Daniel 7:18 and 7:27; readers debate whether they are human, heavenly or both

lessons.title: Power to Become Sons of God
lessons.mainIdea: John 1:12 says that those who received Jesus were given the right to become children of God, using family language that older Jewish texts already used.
reading: The Gospel of John opens with a poem about the Word. Near its end comes John 1:12. The King James Version says that to those who received him, 'gave he power to become the sons of God.' The Greek word behind 'power' is *exousia*, which also means right or authority. Many modern translations say 'the right to become children of God.' Verse 13 adds that they are born 'not of blood' or human will, 'but of God.'

The family language is older than John. In the Hebrew Bible the phrase 'sons of God' usually names heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7. But Hosea 1:10 promises that Israel will be called 'the sons of the living God' (KJV), and Paul quotes that verse in Romans 9:26. Jubilees 1:24–25, in Charles's 1917 translation, has God promise that his people will be called children of the living God, and that every angel will know it.

Readers stress different things in John 1:12. Many Christian interpreters focus on the *new birth*: becoming God's child is a gift received by faith, not earned or inherited. Some scholars note that John's Gospel often contrasts birth 'from above' with ordinary birth, as in John 3:3–7. Divine-council readers notice that a title once used for heavenly beings is here given to people. All agree the verse names a new family status that comes from God.

words.d: a Greek word meaning power, right or authority; used in John 1:12
the English for the Greek logos in John 1:1–14, a title John gives to the one who became flesh
being born 'from above' or 'of God,' language found in John 1:13 and John 3:3–7

check.q: What does the Greek word exousia in John 1:12 mean?
check.why: Exousia means power, right or authority, which is why translations differ between 'power' and 'right.'

check.q: According to John 1:13, how are these children born?

check.why: John 1:13 says they are born not of blood or human will, but of God.

lessons.title: Adoption in Romans 8
lessons.mainIdea: Romans 8:14–23 calls believers adopted children of God and pictures all creation waiting for them to be revealed.
reading: Paul wrote Romans around 57 CE to believers in the city of Rome. In Romans 8:14 he says that those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. In verse 15 he says they have received 'the Spirit of *adoption*,' by which they cry 'Abba, Father.' *Abba* is an Aramaic word for father that Jesus himself uses in prayer in Mark 14:36. Paul keeps an Aramaic word inside a Greek letter, which shows how important the family word was to early believers.

Then Paul widens the picture. In Romans 8:19 the whole creation waits eagerly for 'the manifestation of the sons of God,' meaning the moment they are revealed. Verse 22 says creation groans like a woman in labor. Verse 23 says believers groan too, 'waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.' So adoption is both now and not yet: already given, and still to be completed.

Paul's hope has roots in the prophets. Isaiah 65:17 promises 'new heavens and a new earth,' and many scholars see Romans 8 drawing on that hope for a renewed creation. Many Christian readers focus on the *resurrection* of the body. Readers interested in the divine council notice that 'sons of God,' once a name for heavenly beings, now names people about to be revealed. The readings overlap: creation and God's children are made whole together.

words.d: legally taking someone into a family as a child with full rights; Paul's picture for becoming God's child
an Aramaic word for father, used by Jesus in Mark 14:36 and by Paul in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6
being raised to life in a renewed body; in Romans 8:23 Paul calls it the redemption of the body

look.title: Now and Not Yet
look.text: Romans 8:15 says believers have already received the Spirit of adoption. Romans 8:23 says they are still waiting for the adoption, the redemption of the body. Scholars often call this tension 'already and not yet': something given now and completed later.
look.prompt: Think of something in ordinary life that is already yours but not yet complete, like an acceptance letter before the first day. How does that help you explain Romans 8:15 and 8:23 together?

check.q: What language is the word Abba?
check.why: Abba is Aramaic for father; Paul keeps it inside his Greek letter in Romans 8:15.

check.q: In Romans 8:19, what is creation waiting for?
choices: The revealing of the sons of God
check.why: Romans 8:19 says creation waits for the manifestation, or revealing, of the sons of God.

check.q: Which prophet's promise of 'new heavens and a new earth' do many scholars hear behind Romans 8?
check.why: Isaiah 65:17 promises new heavens and a new earth, a hope many scholars see in Romans 8.

lessons.title: Heirs in Galatians 4
lessons.mainIdea: Galatians 4:4–7 uses Roman-style adoption to say that believers are no longer slaves but sons and heirs of God.
reading: In Galatians 4:4–5 Paul writes that when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and under the law, so that 'we might receive the adoption of sons.' Verse 7 draws the result: 'thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an *heir* of God through Christ.' In the King James Version 'servant' translates the Greek word for slave. Paul's point is a change of status in a household.

Paul's readers knew *Roman adoption* well. A Roman adopted son took his new father's name, gained his rights and could inherit his estate. Old debts to his former family were set aside. The most famous case was Octavian, adopted in Julius Caesar's will, who became the emperor Augustus. So when Paul said believers were adopted, his audience heard a legal and permanent change: full sons, with a full share.

Paul also says what the Galatians had been before. In Galatians 4:8 (KJV) they 'did service unto them which by nature are no gods.' Verses 3 and 9 call their old masters the 'elements' of the world, Greek stoicheia. Some scholars read these as spiritual powers; others read them as basic principles or rules. Paul's word for adoption, *huiothesia*, appears only in his letters. Many readers stress his argument that belonging to God comes through Christ, not the law of Moses.

words.d: a person who has the right to receive a parent's property or position
a legal act in Rome that made someone a full son, with the father's name, rights and inheritance
the Greek word for adoption as a son, used in the New Testament only by Paul

lessons.title: We Shall Judge Angels
lessons.mainIdea: In 1 Corinthians 6:3 Paul tells believers they will judge angels, a claim that echoes older Jewish hopes that the faithful would share in God's judgment.
reading: In 1 Corinthians 6 Paul is upset that believers in Corinth are taking each other to court. He asks in verse 2 whether they know that the saints will judge the world. Then in verse 3 he asks, 'Know ye not that we shall judge angels?' His argument runs from larger to smaller: people who will judge angels should be able to settle ordinary disputes among themselves. Paul wrote this letter around 55 CE from Ephesus.

Paul does not explain the claim. He treats it as something his readers should already know. Older texts show where it may come from. Daniel 7:22 says 'judgment was given to the saints of the most High' (KJV). The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book from before Paul's time kept in the Septuagint, says in 3:8 that the righteous 'shall judge the nations, and have dominion over the people' (KJV Apocrypha). Many scholars hear these hopes behind Paul's question.

Readers take 'judge' in more than one way. Some say believers will share in the final verdict on *fallen angels*, such as those in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6, which draw on 1 Enoch's Watchers. Others read 'judge' as 'rule' or 'govern,' as the word sometimes means in the Hebrew Bible, where the judges were leaders. Divine-council readers link the verse with Psalm 82, where God judges gods who judged badly. All agree the verse gives believers a surprising future role.

words.d: holy ones; in Paul's letters, a common name for all believers
to decide a case; in the Hebrew Bible it can also mean to lead or govern
heavenly beings who, in texts like 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6, sinned and are held for judgment

look.title: Paul's Question in Corinth

look.prompt: Paul uses a 'how much more' argument. Rewrite it in your own words as: If this big thing is true, then surely this small thing is true.

check.q: Which Jewish book in the Septuagint says the righteous 'shall judge the nations'?
check.why: Wisdom of Solomon 3:8 says the righteous shall judge the nations and have dominion over the people.

check.q: Which is one other way readers take 'judge' in this verse?

lessons.title: Rule Over the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 2:26–27 and 3:21 promise the one who overcomes a share in Jesus's rule over the nations and a seat on his throne.
reading: Revelation 2–3 holds seven short letters to churches in Asia Minor, in what is now western Turkey. Each ends with a promise 'to him that overcometh.' The letter to Thyatira (Revelation 2:26–27) promises 'power over the nations' and borrows the words of Psalm 2:9: he will rule them with a rod of iron, and they will be broken like a potter's vessels. The letter to Laodicea (Revelation 3:21) promises a seat with Jesus on his throne.

Psalm 2 was a *royal psalm*. In it God tells his anointed king, 'Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance' (Psalm 2:8, KJV). The word 'heathen' there translates the Hebrew *goyim*, meaning nations. Revelation takes the promise made to the king and shares it with those who overcome. Readers who study the divine council see here the nations of Deuteronomy 32 coming back under God's rule, shared with his people.

The picture of breaking pottery can sound harsh. Many commentators note that in the ancient world a shepherd's rod both guided and protected, and that Revelation's Greek verb in 2:27 can mean 'shepherd.' Others read the image as final justice against oppression. Interpreters also differ on when this rule happens: in a future reign on earth, in a heavenly reign now, or in both. The letters themselves stress faithfulness under pressure.

words.d: to win or stay faithful through hardship; the promises in Revelation 2–3 go 'to him that overcometh'
a Hebrew word for nations or peoples, often other than Israel
a psalm about Israel's king, such as Psalm 2 or Psalm 110

check.q: What does Revelation 3:21 promise the one who overcomes?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word goyim mean?
check.why: Goyim means nations or peoples; the KJV of Psalm 2:8 renders it 'heathen.'

lessons.title: Jesus Quotes Psalm 82
lessons.mainIdea: In John 10:34–36 Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, 'Ye are gods,' and ancient and modern readers disagree about who those gods are.
reading: In John 10 a crowd in the temple courts accuses Jesus of blasphemy for making himself God. Jesus answers by quoting Psalm 82:6: 'Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?' (John 10:34). He goes on: if scripture called them gods 'unto whom the word of God came,' and scripture cannot be broken, why accuse him for saying 'I am the Son of God'? (John 10:35–36). The argument moves from the lesser case to the greater.

Psalm 82 was already being read in different ways in Jesus's time. A Dead Sea Scroll known as 11QMelchizedek applies Psalm 82:1, God standing in the divine assembly, to Melchizedek, a heavenly figure who brings judgment. Later rabbinic writings connect verse 6 with Israel at Sinai, when the people received the Torah. The early Christian writer Justin Martyr read the verse as said of humans made worthy by God.

Modern readers identify the 'gods' in three main ways. Many Christian commentators, especially from the Reformation onward, read them as human judges who acted for God. Mullen's study (1980) and many later scholars read Psalm 82 as a *divine council* scene with heavenly beings, the *elohim* who ruled the nations and failed. Michael Heiser held this view too. He argued that Jesus's point is that scripture itself uses elohim for beings other than Israel's God.

Critics of the heavenly reading ask why 'unto whom the word of God came' would fit heavenly beings. Scholars on each side have offered answers, and the debate continues. Whatever the reading, Jesus's point in John 10 stays the same: the crowd's charge does not fit their own scripture.

words.d: a Hebrew word that can mean God, gods or heavenly beings, depending on the passage
the gathering of heavenly beings around God, which many scholars see in Psalm 82
speech that dishonors God; the charge the crowd raises in John 10:33
a Dead Sea Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 that reads Psalm 82:1 about Melchizedek as a heavenly judge

lessons.title: Theosis in Eastern Orthodoxy
lessons.mainIdea: Eastern Orthodox Christians teach theosis, being united with God by grace, and they read it as sharing God's life, never becoming God by nature.
reading: In the early 300s CE, Athanasius, who became bishop of Alexandria in Egypt, wrote a short book called On the Incarnation. In one famous line he says, in a paraphrase, that God became human so that humans might become divine. Eastern Orthodox Christians use the word *theosis*, or deification, for this idea. They often pair it with 2 Peter 1:4, which speaks of becoming 'partakers of the divine nature' (KJV).

Athanasius was not the first. More than a century earlier, Irenaeus of Lyons wrote in Against Heresies that Christ became what humans are so that he might bring them to be what he is. English readers can find it in the Ante-Nicene Fathers series (1885–87). Irenaeus also quoted Psalm 82:6, 'I said, Ye are gods,' in the same work. So the church fathers were already reading the psalm as a promise about people.

Orthodox teachers are careful about what theosis means. It is union with God by *grace*, a gift, not a change into God's own being. In the 1300s the monk and bishop Gregory Palamas described this with a distinction between God's *essence*, which no creature can share, and God's energies, his active presence, which humans can share. An iron in a fire is a common Orthodox picture: the iron glows with the fire's heat but remains iron.

Western Christian traditions tend to use other words, such as glorification or sanctification, and some are cautious about the term theosis. Some modern readers compare theosis with divine-council readings of Psalm 82, since both speak of humans raised into a share of God's life and rule. Comparing them shows different traditions working on the same biblical passages.

words.d: an Eastern Orthodox teaching that humans are united with God and share his life by grace; also called deification
God's free gift, not earned; in theosis, the way humans share God's life
what a being is in itself; Gregory Palamas taught that God's essence cannot be shared, though his energies can
the Christian teaching that the Son of God became a human being

check.why: Irenaeus wrote this in Against Heresies, more than a century before Athanasius.

lessons.title: Children of God in Jewish Readings
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew Bible calls Israel God's son and children, and Jewish tradition reads this as a covenant bond of love and duty, not as becoming divine.
reading: In Exodus 4:22 God sends a message to Pharaoh through Moses: 'Israel is my son, even my firstborn' (KJV). Deuteronomy 14:1 tells the people, 'Ye are the children of the LORD your God.' Hosea 11:1 remembers God calling his son out of Egypt. In these verses the whole people is God's child. The family language belongs to Israel long before the New Testament uses it.

Jewish tradition has usually read this family bond through the *covenant*, the binding agreement at Sinai. Being God's children brings closeness and also duty: to keep the commandments and to live as a holy people. A famous saying of Rabbi Akiva in the *Mishnah*, in Pirkei Avot chapter 3, says that Israel is beloved because they are called children of God, and it was an extra sign of love that they were told so. The saying treats the title as love made known, not a change in nature.

Jewish readers generally do not describe people becoming divine, and the strong teaching of God's oneness in the *Shema* (Deuteronomy 6:4) shapes that. Christian readings build on the same Hebrew verses but apply the family language to all who trust in Jesus, from every nation. Comparing the readings shows where they share roots and where they part ways.

words.d: a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel made at Sinai
Deuteronomy 6:4, 'Hear, O Israel,' the central Jewish statement that God is one
the first major written collection of Jewish oral law, completed around 200 CE

lessons.title: Never Equal to God
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient texts promise the faithful a shining future beside the heavenly hosts, and readers across traditions insist they never become equal to God.
reading: Several ancient texts picture the faithful raised very high. Daniel 12:3 says the wise 'shall shine as the brightness of the firmament' and 'as the stars for ever and ever' (KJV). In 1 Enoch 104, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, the righteous are promised that they will shine like the lights of heaven and become companions of the hosts of heaven. Jesus says in Matthew 22:30 that in the resurrection people are 'as the angels of God in heaven.'

Yet the same texts keep a line between the faithful and God. 1 John 3:2 says believers will be 'like him' when he appears; being like someone is not being him. Romans 8:29 calls Jesus 'the firstborn among many brethren': a family with an eldest, not a crowd of equals. Shining like stars or keeping company with angels still leaves the faithful as creatures who worship God, not beings who replace him.

Researchers who read Psalm 82 as a heavenly council say the same. Michael Heiser argued in The Unseen Realm (2015) that elohim names beings whose home is the unseen realm, not their rank. In his view, only Israel's God is *uncreated* and worthy of worship, and glorified humans remain creatures. Eastern Orthodoxy says humans share God's energies, never his essence. Jewish readings keep God's oneness at the center. Readers who disagree about the council still agree on this line.

words.d: not made by anyone; in the Bible's view, true only of God
raised to honor and a renewed life; Paul's word in Romans 8:30
the eldest child, with a place of honor; used of Jesus in Romans 8:29 and Colossians 1:15

chapters.title: Har Magedon and the New Eden
chapters.bigQuestion: What do Revelation's last chapters say about the final battle and the new Jerusalem, and how do readers ancient and modern understand them?

story.title: The Hill with Cities Inside
story.kicker: On a school trip to Israel, a group stands on the mound of Megiddo and asks where the famous mountain of Armageddon is.
paragraphs: The bus climbed a low road and stopped at the edge of a wide green valley. The tour guide, a patient archaeologist named Dalia, led the students up a path to the top of a flat-topped mound. Below them the Jezreel Valley stretched out in fields of wheat and sunflowers. 'This is Tel Megiddo,' she said. 'A tel is a hill made by people. Every city here was built on top of the ruins of the one before.'

She pointed to a deep trench cut by excavators. In its walls the students could see bands of stone, ash and packed earth, one above another. 'Archaeologists count more than twenty layers of cities here,' Dalia said, 'from long before Israel's kings down to Persian times.' The city guarded an old road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Pharaoh Thutmose III fought a battle here in the 1400s BCE, and 2 Kings 23:29 says King Josiah of Judah died here in 609 BCE.

A student named Marcus raised his hand. 'My grandmother says the last battle happens at Armageddon. Is this it?' Dalia smiled. 'The book of Revelation says the kings gather at a place called in Hebrew Armageddon, or Har Magedon. Har means mountain. Many readers take it to mean the mountain of Megiddo.' Marcus looked around at the gentle mound. 'This is not much of a mountain,' he said.

'You are not the first to notice,' Dalia said. 'Some scholars think the name points somewhere else.' She told them about a phrase in Isaiah 14, the mountain of assembly, where God's council meets. A few scholars, Michael Heiser among them, hear that phrase inside Har Magedon. Other readers see the name as a symbol, drawn from Megiddo's long story of battles.

On the bus home Marcus opened Revelation on his phone. He read past the battle to the last two chapters: a city with a river and a tree, and nations walking in its light. He wrote a note to himself: the book does not end with a battle. It ends with a garden city.
story.think: Why might a name in Revelation carry a hidden meaning from the Hebrew Bible? What would you need to check before trusting such a reading?

lessons.title: One Verse, One Name
lessons.mainIdea: The name Armageddon appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 16:16, as a Greek spelling of a Hebrew place name.
reading: Revelation is the last book of the Christian Bible. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:9). Many scholars date it to around 95 CE, and some date it earlier, near 68 CE. Chapters 15 and 16 describe seven angels pouring out seven *bowls* of judgment. Between the sixth and seventh bowls comes a short scene about a gathering for battle.

In Revelation 16:13–14 John sees three unclean spirits like frogs come from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet. They go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for 'the battle of that great day of God Almighty.' Then verse 16 names the place: 'a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon.' In the Greek of the earliest manuscripts the name is spelled *Harmagedon*. That is the only place the name appears in the whole Bible.

John does not describe the battle in chapter 16. The seventh bowl follows at once, and the battle itself is told later, briefly, in Revelation 19:11–21. Because the name appears only once, readers must work out its meaning from its Hebrew parts. John's words 'in the Hebrew tongue' invite exactly that. The next lessons look at how readers have done it.

words.d: the last book of the New Testament, a book of visions given to John on Patmos
in Revelation 15–16, the seven bowls of judgment poured out by seven angels
the Greek spelling of the place name in Revelation 16:16, usually written Armageddon in English

lessons.title: The Usual Reading: Megiddo
lessons.mainIdea: Most readers take Har Magedon to mean 'mountain of Megiddo,' a city in northern Israel with a long history of battles.
reading: In Hebrew, *har* means mountain or hill. The second part, Magedon, looks like Megiddo, a city at the edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel. So the most common reading is 'mountain of Megiddo.' Megiddo is a *tel*, a mound built up from many layers of ruined cities. Archaeologists count more than twenty of them. It became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.

Megiddo guarded a pass on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, so armies met there again and again. Pharaoh Thutmose III won a famous battle there in the 1400s BCE, recorded on the walls of the temple at Karnak. Judges 5:19 sets a battle 'by the waters of Megiddo.' 2 Kings 23:29 says King Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BCE facing Pharaoh Necho. In 1918 the British general Edmund Allenby fought a battle nearby that took the name Megiddo.

For many readers, that history is the point. John chose a place whose name already meant war, the way a person today might say 'Waterloo' for a final defeat. Futurist readers often expect armies to gather in the Jezreel Valley itself. Symbolic readers see Megiddo as a picture of every final clash between good and evil. Both start from the place name.

words.d: a Hebrew word meaning mountain or hill
a mound formed by layers of ruined towns built one on top of another
a broad, fertile valley in northern Israel, overlooked by Megiddo

look.title: A Name That Means War
look.text: Some place names carry a history. 'Waterloo' in English can mean a final defeat, because of the battle in 1815. Megiddo was a battlefield for Thutmose III, for the story in Judges 5, and for King Josiah. Many readers think John used the name the same way.
look.prompt: Think of a place name that people use to mean more than a place. How does that help explain the usual reading of Revelation 16:16?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word har mean?
check.why: Har is Hebrew for mountain or hill.

check.q: Which king does 2 Kings 23:29 say died at Megiddo?
check.why: 2 Kings 23:29 says Josiah died at Megiddo facing Pharaoh Necho, in 609 BCE.

check.q: Why do many readers think John chose the name Megiddo?
choices: Because it was the tallest mountain in Israel
Because the place already stood for great battles
check.why: Megiddo had a long history of battles, so its name already suggested war.

lessons.title: A Mountain Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Megiddo is a mound on a plain, and no Hebrew Bible text speaks of a Mount Megiddo, which leads some scholars to look for another meaning.
reading: Marcus's comment on the bus trip points to a real problem. Megiddo sits on a mound that rises only modestly above the valley. It is not a mountain in any ordinary sense. The Hebrew Bible speaks of the city of Megiddo, the waters of Megiddo, and the valley or plain of Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:22; Zechariah 12:11). It never speaks of a 'mountain of Megiddo.'

Scholars have answered this in different ways. Some say John meant the hills near Megiddo, such as *Mount Carmel* a few miles to the northwest. Some say the tel itself, after so many cities, was hill enough. Others say the name is *symbolic*, so it need not match any map. A few scholars in the twentieth century suggested that Har Magedon hides a different Hebrew phrase that later readers had mistaken for Megiddo.

This is how careful reading works. A reader notices a detail that does not fit, then asks what would explain it. The answer may be simple or may need more digging. The mountain problem sends some readers back to the Hebrew Bible's language about God's own mountain, where his council meets. That language, and the proposal built on it, is the subject of the next section.

words.d: a ridge of hills in northern Israel near Megiddo, where 1 Kings 18 sets Elijah's contest
standing for an idea rather than for a literal thing or place
the flat land around Megiddo, named in 2 Chronicles 35:22 and Zechariah 12:11

look.title: What the Map Says
look.text: Texts about Megiddo: 'the waters of Megiddo' (Judges 5:19), 'the valley of Megiddo' (2 Chronicles 35:22), 'the valley of Megiddon' (Zechariah 12:11). No text says 'mountain of Megiddo.' Revelation 16:16 says Har Magedon, with har meaning mountain.

check.q: Which hills near Megiddo do some scholars suggest John meant?
check.why: Some scholars point to Mount Carmel, a few miles northwest of Megiddo.

lessons.title: The Mount of Assembly in Isaiah 14
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 14:13 speaks of har mo'ed, the 'mount of assembly' in the far north, a mountain of the gods that a fallen rebel boasts he will climb.
reading: Isaiah 14 is a taunt song against the king of Babylon. In verses 12–15 it turns to a bright figure, called in Hebrew Helel ben Shahar, 'shining one, son of the dawn,' who has fallen from heaven. The Greek Septuagint calls him the morning star, and the Latin Vulgate's word is Lucifer. In verse 13 he boasts that he will sit on 'the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north' (KJV). The Hebrew for that mount is *har mo'ed*, often translated 'mount of assembly.'

Mo'ed means an appointed meeting or assembly. The same word appears in the tent of meeting, where God met Moses. The phrase 'sides of the north' translates the Hebrew *Zaphon*. In the clay tablets found at Ugarit in Syria, Zaphon is the mountain where the god Baal had his palace, and the gods gather in assembly. Psalm 48:2 uses the same word for Mount Zion, calling it beautiful 'on the sides of the north.'

Richard J. Clifford, in The Cosmic Mountain in Canaan and the Old Testament (1972), studied these texts together. He showed how the Hebrew Bible borrows the old picture of a holy mountain where the *divine council* meets. Many interpreters read Isaiah 14:12–15 only as poetry about the Babylonian king's pride. Christian tradition has often connected the shining one with Satan. Either way, the verse names a mountain of assembly.

words.d: Hebrew for 'mount of assembly,' the council's mountain named in Isaiah 14:13
Hebrew for 'north'; also a mountain linked with Baal at Ugarit and used of Mount Zion in Psalm 48:2
the gathering of heavenly beings around God's throne
a poem that mocks a fallen enemy, like Isaiah 14 against the king of Babylon

look.text: For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north.
look.prompt: The boaster wants to climb, rise and sit. What does each verb say about where the mount of the congregation is and what it means to sit there?

check.why: Har mo'ed means mount of assembly, the KJV's 'mount of the congregation.'

check.q: Against which king is Isaiah 14 a taunt song?
check.why: Isaiah 14 taunts the king of Babylon.

check.why: The Ugaritic tablets place Baal's palace on Mount Zaphon, the word Isaiah 14:13 uses for 'the north.'

lessons.title: From Mo'ed to Magedon
lessons.mainIdea: Some scholars, including Michael Heiser, argue that Greek Harmagedon can come from Hebrew har mo'ed, because Greek often wrote the Hebrew letter ayin with a g sound.
reading: How could har mo'ed become Harmagedon? The case rests on one Hebrew letter. Mo'ed begins with m and then has the letter *ayin*, a throat sound that Greek has no letter for. When Greek writers spelled Hebrew names, they sometimes wrote ayin as a g. This kind of spelling across alphabets is called *transliteration*. The city Hebrew calls 'Amorah became Gomorrah. The city Hebrew calls 'Azzah became Gaza. Both g sounds stand for ayin.

So a Hebrew phrase like har mo'ed, spelled in Greek letters, could come out close to har-mog-ed, and with a common ending, Harmagedon. Earlier scholars had proposed this, and Michael Heiser defended it in The Unseen Realm (2015). He argued that John, who says the name is 'in the Hebrew tongue,' was pointing readers to the mount of assembly. If so, the last battle is about God's own *cosmic mountain*, which the Hebrew Bible also calls Zion.

Scholars weigh this carefully. Supporters note that it solves the mountain problem and fits Revelation's many echoes of Isaiah. Critics note that the spelling match is not exact and that Megiddo remains the simpler explanation of the Greek. Most commentaries on Revelation still favor Megiddo. Like much in Revelation, the name remains debated, and a careful reader can lay both proposals side by side.

words.d: a letter of the Hebrew alphabet with a throat sound that Greek had no letter for
writing a word from one language in the letters of another, like Hebrew names in Greek
the idea, common in the ancient Near East, of a holy mountain where heaven and earth meet and the gods meet

look.title: Following One Letter
look.text: Hebrew 'Amorah (with ayin) became Greek Gomorrha. Hebrew 'Azzah (with ayin) became Greek Gaza. Hebrew har mo'ed (with ayin after the m) could become Greek Har-mag-ed. Some scholars read Harmagedon this way. Most commentaries read it as Har + Megiddo.
look.prompt: Lay the two explanations side by side. Which letters does each one explain well, and which does it struggle with?

choices: They always left it as ayin
check.why: Greek sometimes wrote ayin as g, as in Gomorrah and Gaza.

check.q: Which city name shows ayin becoming a g in Greek?
check.why: Hebrew 'Azzah, which begins with ayin, became Greek Gaza.

check.q: What is one objection critics raise against the har mo'ed reading that Heiser defended?

lessons.title: The Powers' Last Stand
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 16:13–14 and 20:7–9 gather the nations against the beloved city, drawing on prophets who set the last battle at Jerusalem.
reading: Revelation 16:13–14 says three unclean spirits go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for battle. Revelation 20:8 names the gathered nations 'Gog and Magog,' borrowing the names from Ezekiel 38–39, where Gog leads many peoples against Israel. Revelation 20:9 says they surround 'the camp of the saints about, and the beloved city.' Then fire comes down from heaven, and it is over.

The prophets had set the last battle at Jerusalem. Zechariah 14:2 says God will gather all nations against Jerusalem. Joel 3:2 speaks of gathering the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat. Psalm 2 pictures the kings of the earth raging against the LORD's king set on his holy hill of *Zion*. Many scholars see Revelation weaving these passages together, as it does throughout the book.

Michael Heiser read the gathering as the last stand of the powers who had ruled the nations since Babel, aimed at God's own mountain. He drew a contrast with Mount *Hermon*, where 1 Enoch 6 says the Watchers came down and swore their oath. In his reading, a story that began with rebellion on one mountain ends at another. Futurist readers often expect a literal gathering of armies. Idealist readers see a picture of the end of all evil.

words.d: a high mountain north of Israel; 1 Enoch 6 says the Watchers descended there
the hill of Jerusalem, often used in the Bible for God's holy mountain and dwelling
names from Ezekiel 38–39 that Revelation 20:8 uses for the nations gathered for the last battle

look.title: Two Mountains
look.text: 1 Enoch 6 says the Watchers came down on Mount Hermon and swore an oath together. Revelation 20:9 says the nations surround the beloved city, and fire from heaven ends the battle. Heiser read the Bible's story as moving from rebellion at Hermon to victory at Zion.

Only human armies with no background
check.why: Heiser read Revelation 16:13–14 as the fallen gods of the nations rallying the kings for a last stand.

check.q: Which prophet's chapters give Revelation 20:8 the names Gog and Magog?

lessons.title: The Dragon Bound
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 20 tells of Satan bound for a thousand years, a scene that echoes 1 Enoch 10, and readers since the church fathers have held different views of that thousand years.
reading: Revelation 20:1–3 describes an angel coming down with the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain. He seizes the dragon, whom the text names 'that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan,' and binds him for a thousand years so he cannot deceive the nations. After that, verses 7–10 say, he is released briefly and then thrown into the lake of fire. The words 'old serpent' point back to the serpent of Eden, the *nachash* of Genesis 3.

An older Jewish text has a similar scene. In 1 Enoch 10, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, God tells the angel Raphael to bind Azazel hand and foot and cast him into the darkness until the great day of judgment. Michael is told to bind Semjaza and his companions. Many scholars compare these bindings with Revelation 20, where a rebel is chained and held until a final judgment.

The thousand years is called the *millennium*, from Latin for a thousand years. Justin Martyr, in his Dialogue with Trypho (c. 155 CE), expected a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem. Augustine, in The City of God (Book 20, c. 426 CE), read the thousand years as the present age of the church. Today premillennial readers expect Jesus to return before a literal reign on earth, postmillennial readers expect the reign before his return, and *amillennial* readers follow a view like Augustine's.

words.d: the Hebrew word for the serpent in Genesis 3; Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 call the dragon 'that old serpent'
the thousand years of Revelation 20, from the Latin for a thousand years
the view that Jesus returns before a literal thousand-year reign
the view that the thousand years is a symbol of the present age

lessons.title: A City Shaped Like a Cube
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 21:16 describes the new Jerusalem as equal in length, width and height, like the cube-shaped holy of holies in Solomon's temple.
reading: In Revelation 21 John sees 'a new heaven and a new earth' and the new Jerusalem coming down from God. An angel measures the city with a golden reed. Revelation 21:16 says the city 'lieth foursquare' and that its length, breadth and height are equal: twelve thousand furlongs, or *stadia*, each way. That is roughly 1,400 miles. The shape is a cube, or possibly a pyramid, though most readers take it as a cube.

The Hebrew Bible has one famous cube. 1 Kings 6:20 says the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, the *holy of holies*, was twenty cubits long, twenty wide and twenty high. That room held the ark of the covenant and was where God's presence was said to dwell. Only the high priest entered it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). John's city takes the holy of holies' shape and makes it the size of a whole world.

Revelation 21:22 then says John saw no temple in the city, because God and the Lamb are its temple. Revelation 21:3 says the dwelling of God is with humans. G. K. Beale, in The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004), argued that the whole new creation becomes a temple, the goal that Eden and the tabernacle had pointed toward. Many readers across traditions agree the cube points to the holy of holies, even when they read the numbers symbolically.

words.d: the innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, where God's presence was said to dwell

lessons.title: A Garden in the City
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 22:1–3 fills the city with a river and the tree of life, echoing Eden, Ezekiel and an older scene in 1 Enoch of a tree beside God's mountain throne.
reading: Revelation 22 opens with a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. On either side of the river stands the *tree of life*, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month. Verse 3 says there will be no more *curse*. Each of these details echoes Genesis 2–3, where a river flows out of Eden (Genesis 2:10), the tree of life grows in the garden (2:9), and the curse follows the first rebellion (3:14–19).

Other texts had already placed Eden on a mountain. Ezekiel 28:13–14 calls *Eden* 'the garden of God' and speaks of 'the holy mountain of God.' In 1 Enoch 24–25 (Charles, 1917), Enoch sees a high mountain like a throne, where God will sit when he comes down. Beside it grows a fragrant tree no one may touch until the judgment. Then its fruit will be given to the righteous and planted near the house of God.

Ezekiel 47 gives another parallel: a river flows from the temple and trees grow along its banks, with fruit every month and leaves for healing (Ezekiel 47:12). Many scholars see John drawing on Genesis, Ezekiel and wider Jewish hopes like those in 1 Enoch. Readers differ on whether Revelation 22 describes a literal renewed earth, a heavenly reality, or a picture of life with God. They widely agree the story that began in a garden ends in a garden city.

lessons.title: Healing for the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation 21–22 shows the nations walking in the city's light and healed by the tree's leaves, drawing on Isaiah's hope that the nations would come to God's mountain.
reading: Revelation 22:2 says the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations.' Revelation 21:24 says the nations will walk in the city's light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Verse 25 says its gates will never be shut. Earlier, Revelation 7:9 describes a crowd from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne.

The prophets had hoped for this. Isaiah 2:2–3 pictures many peoples streaming to the mountain of the LORD's house. Isaiah 60:3 says the Gentiles shall come to Zion's light and kings to its brightness, and Isaiah 60:11 says its gates shall be open continually (KJV). Revelation 21:24–26 takes up these lines closely. The nations once scattered at Babel (Genesis 11) now come to God's city in peace.

Readers stress different parts of the scene. Richard Bauckham, in The Climax of Prophecy (1993), argued that Revelation hopes for the conversion of the *nations*, not only their defeat. Readers who study the divine council see the ending of the Babel story, with the powers that led the nations astray removed. Some focus on the church drawn from every people; others on healed cultures bringing their 'glory and honor' in. Across readings, the twelve open *gates* picture a welcome rather than a wall.

lessons.title: Four Approaches
lessons.mainIdea: Readers approach Revelation in four main ways, preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist, and many combine them.
reading: Revelation has been read in many ways, and scholars usually group them into four approaches. A *preterist* reading, from Latin for past, holds that most of the book describes events of John's own time, such as Rome's persecution of Christians or the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. A *historicist* reading holds that the book maps out church history from John's day to the end. Many Protestant Reformers read it this way.

A *futurist* reading holds that most of the book, from chapter 4 onward, describes events still to come before the end. This view is widespread among evangelical Christians in the United States today. An *idealist* reading holds that the book pictures timeless truths, the struggle of good and evil and God's final victory, rather than particular events. Each approach can point to features of the text that support it.

Many modern scholars mix approaches. They read Revelation first as a letter to seven real churches in the first century (Revelation 1:4), then ask what it hoped for beyond that. Researchers who study the Hebrew Bible background, from Clifford on the cosmic mountain to Heiser on the divine council, offer material that any approach can use: the nations, the holy mountain and Eden. Their readings of Har Magedon and the new Jerusalem can fit more than one of the four.

words.d: reading Revelation as mostly about events of John's own time
reading Revelation as a map of church history from John's day to the end
reading most of Revelation as describing events still to come

lessons.title: Reading Revelation Calmly
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation is written in symbols drawn from the Hebrew Bible, and careful readers check claims against the text rather than headlines.
reading: Revelation uses numbers as patterns. There are seven letters, seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls. Twelve returns in the gates, the foundations and the tree's fruit. Many scholars read seven as completeness and twelve as God's people, from Israel's twelve tribes. This is not a code to be cracked with dates. It is a way of writing called *apocalyptic*, full of symbols, that many Jewish books of the time also used, such as Daniel and 1 Enoch.

Over the centuries, many people have announced that Revelation's battles were about to happen in their own day, naming leaders and dates. Those predictions have not come true. Ancient readers already urged care. Irenaeus, in Against Heresies (Book 5), discussed the number 666 but advised waiting rather than guessing a name. Augustine, in The City of God (Book 18), warned against trying to calculate the time of the end.

A careful reader can ask three questions of any claim about Revelation. What does the text actually say, in which verse? What Hebrew Bible passage does it echo? Who holds this reading, and who reads it differently? The book itself ends not with fear but with an invitation, 'Come' (Revelation 22:17), and with God wiping away tears (Revelation 21:4). Readers of every approach notice that ending.

words.d: a kind of ancient writing that reveals hidden realities through visions and symbols, as in Daniel, 1 Enoch and Revelation
an image or number that stands for an idea, such as seven for completeness
presented to shock or excite rather than to inform
